items.prompt: Two processes both have a pointer with the same value, 0x7fff1000. Why doesn't reading through it in process A ever accidentally return data from process B?
choices: The OS randomizes every pointer value at allocation time so two processes can never collide on the same number
Each process has its own page table — the same virtual address maps to a different (or no) physical location per process
Processes share physical memory directly, but the CPU's cache hardware silently blocks any cross-process read
It's mostly coincidence that it works — under heavy load it occasionally does leak data between two processes
items.explanation: Addresses are never physical from a process's point of view. The MMU translates every virtual address through that specific process's page table, so identical virtual addresses in two processes almost always resolve to entirely different physical memory — often none at all.
items.reflection: Process isolation is the same guarantee under different names in a lot of places: a sandboxed iframe, a container's own filesystem namespace, a VM's own kernel. Where else have you relied on "this can't see that" turning out to be a structural guarantee enforced by hardware/software, rather than just a convention everyone happens to follow?

choices: Tab B's copy of the script simply has a typo in the variable name, so it never actually reads `counter`
Tabs run as separate processes (or process-like isolates), each with its own private memory — there was never one shared `counter` to begin with
The browser deliberately hides changes between tabs as pure security theater, with no real technical mechanism behind it
JavaScript variables are always read-only the second time a script is re-run in any execution context
items.explanation: Each tab's `counter` lives in that tab's own process memory. "Setting it in tab A" and "reading it in tab B" were never operating on the same storage — this is process isolation, the same mechanism that keeps any two unrelated processes from stepping on each other's memory.

No — virtual address ranges are private per process; two processes legitimately reusing the same range (e.g. both mapping their own text segment there) is completely ordinary and implies nothing about physical memory
Yes, but only if both processes were started by the same user account
No, but only because ASLR (address space layout randomization) happens to make this impossible on modern systems
items.explanation: Virtual address ranges aren't a shared resource to collide over — every process gets its own, so two processes reporting overlapping-looking ranges is exactly what you'd expect, not evidence of a leak.

items.prompt: Process X writes the string "secret" to virtual address 0x5000. Process Y, running at the same time, reads virtual address 0x5000. What does Y most likely get?
choices: Y gets back the exact string "secret", since both processes are reading from the same shared address
Whatever Y's own page table maps 0x5000 to, unrelated to X's write — very likely not "secret"
Y always gets a permission error instead of a value, with no exceptions across any operating system
Y gets back half of X's data interleaved with its own memory contents at that same address
items.explanation: 0x5000 is only a number until it passes through a page table. X's page table and Y's page table almost certainly map 0x5000 to different physical pages (or Y's mapping may not even exist), so Y's read has no relationship to what X wrote.

items.prompt: Does a process's memory belong to that process alone, by default?
choices: Yes — private unless explicitly shared
No — any process can read any other's memory
Only on Windows
Only if both run as root
items.explanation: Private-by-default is the whole point of process isolation; sharing has to be requested explicitly (e.g. shared memory segments).

items.prompt: Two terminal windows run `python script.py` at the same time. Do the two runs share a heap?
choices: Yes, always
No — each is its own process with its own heap
Only the first 1MB
Only if the script imports the same modules
items.explanation: Running the same program twice creates two separate processes, each with its own private heap — the source code being identical changes nothing about memory ownership.

items.prompt: If process A could freely read process B's memory just by guessing addresses, what would that represent?
choices: Normal, expected behavior
A serious isolation failure / security vulnerability
A performance optimization
Standard multithreading
items.explanation: The entire point of per-process page tables is to make this impossible under normal circumstances — if it worked, it would be a major security bug.

items.prompt: What does it mean that a virtual address is "private" to a process?
choices: It's encrypted so other processes can't decrypt it
It only has meaning when translated through that process's own page table
It's stored on a private disk partition
It can only be read once
items.explanation: Privacy here is structural, not cryptographic: the address is just a number until a specific page table resolves it, and only that process's table resolves it meaningfully for that process.

items.prompt: A script sets a global variable to 42 in one process. A completely separate process, running different code, checks "the same" variable name. What will it see?
choices: 42, inherited automatically
Whatever that process's own copy (if any) holds — nothing automatically carries over
An error, always
0, always, regardless of the second process's own code
items.explanation: Unrelated processes don't share variables at all; whatever the second process sees depends entirely on its own code and memory, not the first process's state.

items.prompt: True or false: process isolation is enforced by convention — well-behaved programs just agree not to peek at each other's memory.
choices: True
False — it's enforced structurally via page tables and the MMU, not politeness
items.explanation: It's not a gentlemen's agreement — a process physically cannot express a pointer that resolves into another process's memory without a deliberate, OS-sanctioned shared mapping.

items.prompt: Which of these would actually let two processes share data on purpose?
choices: Both happening to use the same variable name
An explicitly requested shared memory mapping (e.g. POSIX shared memory)
Running on the same CPU core
Starting them at the same time
items.explanation: Sharing is always an opt-in, explicit request to the kernel to map the same physical pages into both processes — never an accident of naming or timing.

items.prompt: Two unrelated processes each allocate a variable and both happen to get assigned the identical virtual address by their own allocators. Is this a problem?
choices: Yes — this always causes memory corruption
No — virtual addresses are scoped per-process, so an identical number in two processes is not a collision
Only if they're both written in the same programming language
Yes, but only on 32-bit systems
items.explanation: Collision only matters within the same page table. The same virtual address number in two different processes is just two unrelated numbers that happen to look alike.

items.prompt: A program dereferences a NULL pointer and crashes immediately instead of silently reading garbage data. Why?
choices: NULL is a special CPU instruction opcode that the processor is hardwired to always treat as a crash
Address 0x0 is deliberately left unmapped in the process's page table, so any access to it faults
The compiler inserts an explicit runtime check before every single pointer dereference in the compiled binary
RAM physically has no storage cells at address zero, so the hardware itself refuses the access automatically
items.explanation: Leaving 0x0 unmapped is a deliberate OS/loader decision, not a hardware property of RAM — it turns a whole class of bugs (using a pointer before it's set to something real) into an immediate, loud fault instead of a silent read of unrelated memory.
items.reflection: "Fail loudly and immediately" vs. "silently keep going with bad data" is a design choice that shows up far beyond NULL pointers — a strict schema that rejects an unexpected field vs. one that quietly ignores it, a type system that refuses to compile vs. one that coerces. Where have you seen a system choose the loud failure on purpose, and was it the right call?

items.prompt: If the OS instead mapped a real, readable page at address 0x0 (rather than leaving it unmapped), what would change about NULL-pointer bugs?
choices: Nothing would change — NULL-pointer bugs would still crash in exactly the same visible way as before
They'd become silent — the program would read whatever happens to be at that page instead of crashing, making the bug much harder to notice
The program would actually run measurably faster, since the CPU would need to raise far fewer page faults
It's not physically possible for any operating system to ever map a page at address 0x0
items.explanation: The crash isn't inherent to the number 0 — it's inherent to that address being unmapped. If it were mapped, a NULL dereference would just read whatever's on that page and keep running with corrupted-looking data, which is strictly worse for debugging than an immediate fault.
items.reflection: "Fail loudly and immediately" vs. "silently keep going with bad data" is a design choice that shows up far beyond NULL pointers — a strict schema that rejects an unexpected field vs. one that quietly ignores it, a type system that refuses to compile vs. one that coerces. Where have you seen a system choose the loud failure on purpose, and was it the right call?

items.prompt: A pointer variable is declared but never assigned a value, and the language doesn't default it to NULL/0 — it's left pointing at whatever garbage bits happened to be in that memory already. How does this differ from a true NULL dereference?
choices: It's identical — both always crash at the exact same guaranteed address
It's worse in a sense — the pointer might point at a mapped, valid page by sheer accident, so the bug can silently "work" sometimes and corrupt memory other times, instead of reliably faulting
It's actually safer, since uninitialized memory is always unmapped by every OS
This situation is impossible in any real programming language
items.explanation: NULL's reliability comes specifically from 0x0 being deliberately and consistently left unmapped. An uninitialized pointer holding random garbage has no such guarantee — it might land on a valid page and silently misbehave instead of faulting, which is a much harder bug to catch.

Where have you seen a system choose the loud failure on purpose, and was it the right call?

items.prompt: What's at virtual address 0x0 in a normal process's page table?
choices: A fast-access cache
Nothing — it's deliberately left unmapped
The process's own PID
The kernel's own code
items.explanation: Address zero is intentionally left unmapped specifically so NULL dereferences fault instead of silently reading garbage.

items.prompt: True or false: a NULL pointer dereference faulting is a hardware accident, not a deliberate design choice.
choices: True
False — it's a deliberate choice by the OS/loader to leave 0x0 unmapped
items.explanation: This is intentional: an unmapped page at address 0 turns a common bug into a loud, immediate, debuggable crash.

items.prompt: Which is easier to debug: a NULL dereference that crashes instantly, or one that silently reads garbage and keeps running?
choices: The crash — you know immediately where and when it happened
The silent garbage read — it gives you more information
They're equally easy
Neither is debuggable
items.explanation: An immediate crash points you straight at the offending line; silently reading garbage can let corrupted data propagate far from its actual cause before anything visibly breaks.

items.prompt: What signal does the kernel send to a process that dereferences an unmapped address like NULL?
choices: SIGSEGV
SIGKILL only, never SIGSEGV
No signal — it just returns an error code
SIGHUP
items.explanation: SIGSEGV ("segmentation violation") is the signal delivered for an access to memory with no valid mapping, including NULL.

items.prompt: Is leaving address 0 unmapped a universal law of computing, or a specific OS design choice?
choices: A universal law — every OS on every architecture must do this
A specific, deliberate design choice most operating systems make
It's random per individual machine
It was outlawed by an official standards body
items.explanation: It's a convention most OSes follow on purpose because it's useful for catching bugs — not a hard physical requirement.

items.prompt: A pointer is set to NULL and then dereferenced inside a managed runtime like JavaScript (reading a property of `null`). Is the underlying reason it fails related to the OS's unmapped-page mechanism?
choices: Yes, directly and always — it's literally the same SIGSEGV
Not directly — managed runtimes typically catch this themselves in software and raise their own catchable error, before the OS mechanism would ever trigger
No, JavaScript has no concept of NULL at all
Yes, but only in server-side JavaScript, never in a browser
items.explanation: A managed runtime like JS checks for null/undefined access in software and raises its own catchable TypeError — similar philosophy to the OS's unmapped-page guard, but enforced earlier and more gracefully, not the literal same mechanism.

items.prompt: Why specifically address 0, and not some other arbitrary address, for the NULL convention?
choices: 0 is simply a convenient, easy-to-check sentinel value that's extremely unlikely to be a real, intentionally-used address
0 is the only address the CPU is physically capable of leaving unmapped
0 was chosen at random with no particular reasoning
Address 0 is where the kernel itself always lives
items.explanation: 0 is just a convenient, recognizable sentinel for "no real address assigned yet" — any consistently-unmapped address could in principle serve the same purpose.

items.prompt: A function is supposed to return a pointer to found data, or NULL if nothing was found. The caller forgets to check for NULL before using the result. What's the likely outcome if nothing was found?
choices: The program silently continues as if data were found, with no visible error
A fault/crash, pointing at the exact line that dereferenced the unchecked NULL
The function call itself fails to compile
Nothing — unchecked NULL is always automatically safe
items.explanation: Dereferencing the unchecked NULL hits the unmapped page and faults — not a silent failure, a loud one right at the point of the mistake.

items.prompt: Which region of a process's address space holds the compiled machine code, and why is it typically marked read-only?
choices: The heap, because code is really just read-write data that happens to get allocated once at process startup
The text segment — read-only so a bug can't accidentally overwrite the program's own instructions
The stack, since the compiled instructions live right alongside the currently executing call frame
The data/bss segment, simply because that's the first region the loader maps into memory
items.explanation: The text segment holds the compiled instructions. Marking it read-only means a stray write (a buffer overrun, a bad pointer) can corrupt data or crash the process, but it can't rewrite the program's own logic on the fly.
items.reflection: Splitting one resource into regions with different permissions and growth rules — code read-only, globals fixed, two growable areas kept apart — is a pattern that repeats outside memory too: a filesystem with read-only system paths vs. writable user paths, a database schema with immutable audit columns vs. mutable ones. Where else have you seen "give different parts of the same resource different rules" solve a real problem?

items.prompt: A function allocates an object with `new` and another calls itself recursively 1000 times. Which two regions grow to accommodate these, respectively?

The heap grows for the `new` allocation; the stack grows for the recursive calls
The stack grows for the `new` allocation; the heap grows for the recursive calls
Both grow the data/bss segment
items.explanation: Dynamic allocation (`new`, `malloc`) always comes from the heap. Function calls — including recursive ones — push frames onto the stack, one per call, regardless of what the function does internally.

items.prompt: Why are the stack and heap conventionally placed at opposite ends of the same free memory region, growing toward each other?
choices: It's purely an arbitrary historical convention, chosen with no real technical reason behind the layout
So neither one needs a fixed size chosen up front — each can grow as needed until they'd eventually collide
To make debugging intentionally harder by keeping the stack's and heap's addresses close together
Because the CPU's memory controller has a hardware requirement that stack and heap sit adjacent to each other
items.explanation: Placing them at opposite ends of shared free space means neither has to be pre-sized — both can grow independently for as long as there's room. It also means their eventual collision (or the stack simply outrunning its reserved space) is exactly what a stack overflow is.

items.prompt: A program has a global array declared at the top of the file (fixed size, known at compile time) and a `Map` it fills at runtime with an unpredictable number of entries. Which regions hold these two, respectively?
choices: The global array lives in data/bss; the runtime-growing Map lives on the heap
Both live in data/bss, since both are declared somewhere in the source code
The global array lives on the heap; the Map lives in data/bss
Both live on the stack, since both are visible to the whole program
items.explanation: A fixed-size global whose size is known at compile time belongs in data/bss. Anything that grows unpredictably at runtime — like a Map filled with an unknown number of entries — has to live on the heap, which is the only region built for that kind of dynamic growth.

False — they're placed at opposite ends of free space so neither needs a pre-chosen size, and collision is the failure mode, not the goal

items.explanation: Unreleased dynamic allocations accumulate on the heap — this is the classic shape of a memory leak.

items.prompt: You run the same script twice in two separate terminal windows. What's true of the two resulting processes?
choices: They end up sharing a single PID between them, since the OS recognizes it's the same underlying program
They get distinct PIDs and separate address spaces, even though they're running identical code
The second launch simply fails outright, because the OS refuses to run the same program a second time
They share the same memory, so changing a variable in one process is immediately visible in the other
items.explanation: A PID identifies a running instance, not a program. Two launches of the same script are two independent processes with two PIDs and two private address spaces — running the same code doesn't mean sharing anything at runtime.
items.reflection: A PID is a disambiguating handle for one specific running instance, not the thing itself — the same pattern shows up anywhere multiple copies of the same "thing" can exist at once: a request ID distinguishing two identical-looking HTTP calls, a primary key distinguishing two rows with the same name. Where have you needed an instance identifier like this, separate from the name of the thing it identifies?

Multiple processes can run the same program simultaneously; a PID is needed to target one specific running instance for operations like sending a signal
PIDs exist purely for log-file formatting purposes, with no functional role in how the OS manages processes
PIDs are actually required by the filesystem itself, as part of how it names and indexes regular files on disk
items.explanation: Program name is ambiguous the moment more than one instance is running. A PID disambiguates: `kill -9 61278` targets exactly one process, where `kill -9 node` wouldn't even be a valid way to express "the second one I started".

Look up each instance's distinct PID (and start time) and send the signal to that specific PID
It's simply not possible to distinguish between identically-named running instances at all
Restart all five processes under different program names first

items.prompt: Does a PID identify a program, or a specific running instance of one?
choices: A program
A specific running instance
A user account
A file on disk
items.explanation: PIDs name instances. Running the same program five times gives five different PIDs.

items.prompt: Can two different processes, running completely different programs, have the same PID at the same time?
choices: Yes, commonly
No — PIDs are unique among currently-running processes
Only on Windows
Only if they were both started by the same command
items.explanation: PIDs are unique among currently-running processes specifically so any one of them can be addressed unambiguously.

items.prompt: `kill -9 61278` sends a signal to...
choices: Every process on the machine named the same as PID 61278's program
The one specific process whose PID is 61278
All processes started by the same user
Nothing — kill -9 requires a program name, not a number
items.explanation: A PID targets exactly one running process, which is precisely why kill commands take a PID rather than a program name.

items.prompt: You launch the same executable three times. How many PIDs get assigned?
choices: One, shared by all three
Three, one per launch
Zero — PIDs are only assigned to the first launch
It depends on whether the terminal windows are different
items.explanation: Each launch creates a new, independent process with its own PID, regardless of how many times the same executable has already been run.

items.prompt: True or false: a PID is reused immediately the instant a process exits.
choices: True, always immediately
False in practice — PIDs are typically not reused until they wrap around after a large range of values
items.explanation: PIDs aren't recycled the instant a process exits; the OS generally allocates PIDs from a large increasing range before wrapping around, reducing accidental collisions with recently-exited processes.

items.prompt: What's the main functional reason the OS assigns a PID at process creation?
choices: So the process has something to print in log messages
So the OS and other tools have a stable way to address that specific running instance for operations like signaling or status lookup
So the filesystem can index the process as a file
There is no real functional reason — it's purely cosmetic
items.explanation: The PID is the OS's functional handle for addressing a process — without it, operations like sending a signal to one specific instance would have no way to target it.

items.prompt: If a tool reports "PID 4821: node, PID 4822: node", what does this tell you?
choices: These are two independent, separately-running instances of the same program
This is a single process that was somehow given two numbers
This is an error — a program can only ever have one PID
Nothing meaningful — PID numbers are random noise
items.explanation: Two distinct PIDs for processes named the same program means two completely separate running instances, each with its own private memory.

items.prompt: What does it mean, precisely, that a process "believes it owns the entire address space"?
choices: The process genuinely does own the entirety of the machine's physical RAM for the whole time that it runs
The process's view of memory is a private illusion maintained by the OS/MMU — its virtual addresses have no necessary relationship to what any other process sees
It means the process is free to read any other running process's memory, provided it tries hard enough to do so
It's essentially a marketing phrase from OS vendors, with no precise technical meaning behind the wording
items.explanation: Virtual memory gives every process the same full private address range to program against, regardless of how many other processes exist or how much physical RAM is actually installed — the OS/MMU handle translating that illusion down to real, shared physical memory behind the scenes.
items.reflection: Giving every consumer a private, full-looking view of a shared resource — while the real allocation happens behind the scenes, only as actually used — is the same trick behind thin-provisioned disks, cloud "unlimited" storage tiers, and even overbooking on a flight. Where else have you seen a system promise more than it could truly give everyone at once, backed by the bet that not everyone claims their share simultaneously?

items.prompt: A machine has 8GB of physical RAM but is running 20 processes, each with its own large virtual address space. How is this possible?

Virtual address space is nearly free to reserve; only the pages a process actually touches get backed by real physical RAM
Each of the 20 processes is secretly and silently capped at only 400MB of usable virtual address space
All 20 processes silently share one single physical address space, with no memory isolation between them at all

Exactly 0 bytes, forever, no matter how much is eventually written

items.explanation: Virtual address space is cheap to reserve; physical RAM is only consumed once a page is actually read or written.

items.prompt: Can two processes legitimately both believe they "own" the full address space at the same time?
choices: No — only one process can hold this illusion at a time
Yes — this illusion is maintained independently per process
Yes, but only if they're run by the same user
No, this concept doesn't apply to more than one process ever
items.explanation: Every process gets this illusion independently — it's a private view the OS/MMU maintains per process, not a machine-wide resource that gets used up.

items.prompt: What actually enforces the virtual-memory illusion for each process?
choices: A written agreement between all running programs
The OS and the CPU's MMU, via per-process page tables
The hard drive's own firmware
Nothing — it's purely a documentation convention
items.explanation: The MMU, guided by each process's page table (which the OS maintains), is the actual mechanism translating virtual addresses into real memory access.

items.prompt: True or false: without virtual memory, every program would need to know at compile time exactly which physical addresses are free.
choices: True

That the large gap between them is unused, wasted RAM the process has permanently reserved
items.explanation: The large numeric gap between the heap's low addresses and the stack's high addresses, visible directly in the kernel's own record, is exactly L2's abstract diagram made concrete — this is the diagram confirmed by live data, not merely asserted.
items.reflection: Reading a system's own internal bookkeeping directly — rather than trusting a diagram or a tool's summary of it — is a habit worth having well beyond /proc/self/maps: reading raw request/response headers instead of trusting a client library's abstraction, reading a database's actual query plan instead of trusting an ORM's claims about what it generates. Where have you gone straight to a system's raw internal record instead of a tool's summary of it, and found something the summary hid?

items.prompt: What is /proc/self/maps, precisely?
choices: A diagram drawn by the documentation team
The kernel's own real record of a process's virtual memory regions, readable as text
A log file the program itself writes
A configuration file set before the process starts
items.explanation: It's the kernel's actual internal bookkeeping about this process's memory layout, exposed as a readable file.

items.prompt: What does a permission string like `rw-p` mean?
choices: Readable, writable, private/copy-on-write, not executable
Read-only, shared, executable
Random, weird, protected
Remote, wired, persistent
items.explanation: Each letter/flag position has a fixed meaning: read, write, execute, and private-vs-shared.

items.prompt: Is the text segment's permission string typically rw-p or r-xp?
choices: rw-p
r-xp
rwxp
items.explanation: Text is readable and executable but not writable — r-xp — which is the hardware-enforced version of "code shouldn't be writable at runtime."

items.prompt: What makes a permission string like rwxp specifically worth flagging as suspicious?
choices: It's simply an uncommon combination of letters
It combines writable and executable at once, which legitimate regions almost never do, and which is exactly what a code-injection exploit needs
The letters are in the wrong alphabetical order
rwxp always indicates the kernel's own memory
items.explanation: Being both writable and executable at once is the specific combination a buffer-overflow-style exploit depends on to write and then run injected code.

items.prompt: Does /proc/self/maps show you a diagram, or a page table's actual contents as text?
choices: A diagram, drawn separately from the real memory layout
The real page-table-derived contents, as text
Neither — it's a cached screenshot
A random sample, not the full record
items.explanation: It's the genuine kernel record, not an illustration — reading it is reading real page-table-derived data.

items.prompt: Does the heap's address range typically sit right next to the stack's, with no gap?
choices: Yes, always adjacent with zero gap
No — there's typically a large gap between them, since they grow from opposite ends of shared free space
Yes, but only on 32-bit systems
The heap doesn't have an address range at all
items.explanation: The large gap between their addresses is exactly what L2's memory-layout diagram predicts — confirmed directly by reading the kernel's own record.

items.prompt: Does the operating system assign a PID when a process is created, or does the program choose its own PID?
choices: The program chooses its own PID
The OS assigns it automatically at creation time
PIDs are assigned by the filesystem
There is no such thing as a PID
items.explanation: PID assignment is entirely the OS's responsibility — a program never gets to pick its own.

items.prompt: Is the full virtual address space a process "sees" the same thing as the physical RAM actually installed on the machine?
choices: Yes, they're always identical
No — the virtual address space is a private illusion, independent of how much physical RAM actually exists
Only on servers, never on desktops
Only for the very first process started
items.explanation: Virtual address space size has no fixed relationship to installed physical RAM — that decoupling is the whole point of the illusion.

items.prompt: If a machine had zero other processes running, would a single process's virtual address space still be a translated illusion, or would it get direct physical access?
choices: It would get direct physical access, since there's no other process to isolate it from
It would still go through virtual-to-physical translation exactly as before — the mechanism doesn't depend on how many other processes exist
It would crash immediately with no other processes present
The OS would disable the MMU in this case
items.explanation: Virtual memory translation is a property of how a process's memory works at all, not a defense mechanism that only activates when other processes are present.

items.prompt: Does writing a network packet to a NIC (network card) count as a privileged operation requiring kernel mode?
choices: No — any user-mode code can directly write to network hardware
Yes — like disk access, it's hardware interaction and has to go through a system call into the kernel
Only on servers, never on laptops
Only if the packet is larger than 1KB
items.explanation: Any direct hardware interaction, networking included, is privileged and has to be requested from the kernel via a system call.

items.prompt: Is the kernel/user mode boundary enforced in software by the OS, or in hardware by the CPU itself?
choices: Purely in software by the OS, with no hardware involvement
Enforced by the CPU's own hardware privilege levels, which the OS relies on
It isn't enforced anywhere — it's just a documentation convention
Only enforced by antivirus software
items.explanation: The CPU itself has hardware-level privilege modes; the OS relies on this hardware enforcement rather than inventing the boundary purely in software.

items.prompt: Is a page table shared across all processes, or private to each one?
choices: Shared by all processes
Private — each process has its own page table
Only shared between parent and child processes
There is only ever one page table per machine
items.explanation: Per-process page tables are exactly what make each process's virtual addresses privately mapped.

items.prompt: True or false: switching which page table the MMU uses is free, with no performance cost at all.
choices: True
False — it can invalidate cached translations (the TLB), making the next several memory accesses more expensive
items.explanation: A context switch's page-table change isn't free — it can force the CPU to re-walk the new process's page table instead of using cached translations.

items.prompt: Does an allocator ever need to ask the OS for more address space to manage, or does it always have enough reserved up front?
choices: It always has enough reserved up front, forever
It can ask the OS (e.g. via brk/mmap) for more virtual address space when it runs low
It can only ever shrink, never grow
This only happens once, at process startup
items.explanation: Heap growth is explicit and request-driven — the allocator asks the OS for more space when its current reservation runs low.

items.prompt: Is stack growth typically bounded by a configured limit (like ulimit -s on Linux), or is it always unlimited by default?
choices: Always unlimited by default on every system
Typically bounded by a configured limit, checked as the stack grows
Stack growth is never actually limited in any way
Only limited on 32-bit systems
items.explanation: Most systems configure a stack size limit (checkable via ulimit -s on Linux) rather than letting the stack grow without bound.

items.prompt: Is a page fault always an error condition?
choices: Yes, always fatal
No — many page faults (lazy allocation, swap-in) are resolved silently and are completely normal
Only on servers
Only if triggered by a write, never by a read
items.explanation: Most page faults in normal operation are benign and handled transparently by the kernel; only ones with no valid mapping become fatal.

items.prompt: What does the kernel's page-fault handler ultimately decide, when a fault occurs?
choices: Whether to reboot the machine
Whether the faulting access has a valid, permitted mapping, or should instead result in SIGSEGV
Which process gets scheduled next
How much disk space is free
items.explanation: The handler's core job on a page fault is distinguishing a resolvable situation (not-yet-backed page) from a genuinely illegitimate access.

items.prompt: Does copy-on-write mean the parent's and child's memory are shared forever, with no real isolation?
choices: Yes — they remain permanently shared
No — sharing is only a temporary, read-only optimization until either side writes, at which point real isolation kicks in via a private copy
Yes, but only for the first 100ms after fork()
No — they're never shared, not even briefly
items.explanation: Sharing is purely a transitional, read-only efficiency measure; isolation is restored the instant either process actually writes to a shared page.

items.prompt: Does process.memoryUsage().heapUsed measure the stack, the heap, or both?
choices: Only the stack
The heap
Both equally
Neither — it measures disk usage
items.explanation: heapUsed is specifically a heap measurement, which is why heap.mjs uses it to prove heap growth, not stack growth.

items.prompt: If heapUsed samples go 10, 20, 30, 40 with no dips at all, does this match the leak signature described in this unit?
choices: No, this doesn't match a leak at all
Yes — monotonically non-decreasing with real net growth is exactly the described leak signature
Only if the values were measured in KB instead of MB
This pattern is impossible in practice
items.explanation: Steady, never-decreasing growth across samples is exactly the practical signature described for a likely leak.

items.prompt: Is /proc/self/maps available identically on plain Windows (without WSL)?
choices: Yes, identical on all platforms
No — plain Windows doesn't expose /proc/self/maps; it has a different diagnostics interface (it works on Linux and usually under WSL)
No OS ever exposes this information
Only available on macOS
items.explanation: This is environment-specific — Linux (including WSL) exposes /proc/self/maps; plain Windows uses different tooling for the same underlying concept.

items.prompt: Does reading /proc/self/maps change or affect the process's actual memory layout?
choices: Yes, reading it resets all mappings
No — it's a read-only view into the kernel's existing record, observing without altering anything
Yes, but only the heap region
It deletes the stack region once read
items.explanation: It's purely observational — reading the kernel's own record doesn't modify the process's actual memory layout in any way.
